page.metaDescription: Track competitor pricing, product launches, hiring, content, and press automatically. One dashboard, real-time alerts on every competitor signal you care about.
page.subtitle: Track competitor product launches, pricing changes, hiring activity, and content publishes from one dashboard. Alerts arrive as the change happens, on the channel the team already watches.
page.intro: Competitor monitoring is the systematic tracking of public-facing signals from your competitors: pricing changes, product launches, hiring activity, content publishes, press coverage, and feature announcements. Done manually, it requires a person checking dozens of pages on a weekly cadence and missing most changes between checks. WebMonitor.fyi automates the polling and alert layer so the signal arrives in real time. Used by product, marketing, sales, and strategy teams to maintain competitive awareness without a dedicated analyst.

features.title: Multi-page competitor coverage
features.body: Pricing page, product page, careers page, blog, press section, changelog — one competitor often spans 6–10 pages worth tracking. Run them all from one dashboard.

features.title: Plain-English criteria
features.body: Write rules like "alert me when this competitor publishes a new blog post about [topic]" or "notify me on any pricing page change".

features.title: Change diffs
features.body: See the exact before/after for each change — what text was added, what was removed, what was reworded. Useful for spotting positioning shifts.

features.title: Multi-competitor dashboards
features.body: Group monitors by competitor. Filter the activity feed by competitor, by page type, or by date range.

features.title: Webhook into Slack
features.body: Most competitive intelligence work lives in Slack. A webhook posts each detected change to a channel with the diff and a link.

steps.title: List the pages worth tracking
steps.body: Start with: pricing, product / features, careers, blog index, press releases, changelog. Add others as relevant (e.g., specific high-stakes product detail pages).

steps.title: Add each as a monitor
steps.body: Paste the URL, write the criterion ("any change", "new entry added", "price changed"), tag it with the competitor name.

steps.title: Pick a frequency
steps.body: Daily is the right default for competitive monitoring. Hourly for pricing pages during a competitor's product launch window.

steps.title: Route to Slack
steps.body: Webhook into a #competitive-intel channel. The team sees every signal in context, without needing to log into another tool.

useCases: Marketing teams catching new positioning copy on competitor sites
Sales teams getting alerts on competitor pricing changes for use in deals
Product teams watching competitor changelogs for feature launches
Talent teams tracking competitor hiring trends and open-role volume
Founders watching for competitor announcements before press picks them up
Investor relations watching for competitor press releases and filings
page.limits: Competitor monitoring sees what competitors publish publicly. Internal strategy decisions, unpublished roadmap, and unannounced launches are outside what any monitoring tool can see. Some competitors A/B test their pricing pages or gate content behind email signups — those are tougher to track reliably.

faq.q: How many competitor pages should I monitor?
faq.a: For most teams, 5–8 pages per competitor covers the high-signal surface: pricing, product, careers, blog, press, changelog. Going past that adds noise faster than signal. Quality of criteria matters more than quantity of monitors.

faq.q: How is this different from a tool like Crayon or Klue?
faq.a: Crayon, Klue, and Kompyte are full competitive intelligence platforms — they include curated battlecards, integrations with CRM, and analyst-prepared summaries. WebMonitor is the alerting layer. Many teams use both: WebMonitor for real-time signal, a CI platform for curated synthesis.

faq.q: Can I monitor competitor LinkedIn or social posts?
faq.a: Public LinkedIn company pages and public Twitter / X profiles work as URLs. Private posts and login-gated content do not. For social monitoring at scale, dedicated social listening tools (Sprout Social, Brand24) cover more ground.

faq.q: What's a good criterion for catching pricing changes?
faq.a: "Alert me on any change to this pricing page" works for most. For specific tier tracking: "Alert me when the price of the Pro plan changes." For new plan launches: "Notify me when a new pricing tier is added."

faq.q: Will my competitors know I'm monitoring them?
faq.a: No. WebMonitor reads public pages with standard web requests; nothing identifying you is sent. The monitoring is invisible to the target.
